title: They Knew in April: The 'Accidental' SpaceX Moon Crash Was Tracked for Months
narrative: On August 3, SpaceX's director of Dragon mission management told a NASA briefing that the Falcon 9 upper stage now slamming into the Moon was 'not deliberate' — the result of 'a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces' — and that 'impacts like this are rare.' NASA added that a meteoroid of the same energy hits the Moon about every six days, so the surface is 'constantly absorbing impacts with the same force.' Today, NASA released imagery of the fresh ~60-foot crater. Independent astronomers had been publishing the collision's trajectory since April — four months before impact — and NASA's own CNEOS had confirmed a 100% chance of impact.
telemetry: Independent astronomer Bill Gray first flagged the projected lunar collision in April using publicly available tracking data — roughly four months of advance warning before the Aug 5 impact (SpaceNews, AP)
Jonathan McDowell tracked the ~4-ton stage: 'no doubt in my mind' the rocket is 'in teeny, little pieces scattered over the moon near Einstein Crater' (AP)
Impact: Aug 5, 2:35 a.m. ET, near Einstein crater on the western limb; ~8,800 lbs traveling ~5,400 mph, energy equivalent of 2-3 tons of TNT (SpaceNews, USA Today)
NASA's CNEOS confirmed 'a 100% chance of impacting the Moon' (CBS)

SpaceX (Julianna Scheiman, Aug 3 NASA briefing): the impact was 'not deliberate'; 'what has happened is essentially a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces have put it on a path toward the moon'; the company followed 'the appropriate rules and regulations' (CBS, SpaceNews)
NASA minimizes the event: 'a meteoroid with the same energy as the upper stage hits the Moon about every six days' (CBS)
Fresh crater imagery (Aug 18): ~60-foot-wide crater at the impact site, confirming the collision occurred exactly where public trackers predicted (CBS)
Korea's Danuri spacecraft released before/after lunar-orbit images showing darkened, cratered terrain (AP, Aug 7)
Scheiman conceded that for high-energy trajectories like this launch, deorbiting the stage 'is not possible' (SpaceNews)
The disposal SpaceX claimed to have handled 'per the appropriate rules and regulations' left a stage in an orbit independent trackers flagged as collision-bound in April
analysis:
The SpaceX moon crash is a case study in how institutions narrate predictable failures as accidents. Every element of the official story — 'not deliberate,' 'rare,' 'solar activity and gravity' — was falsifiable before the impact even happened, using public data.

Start with the timeline. Bill Gray, an independent astronomer, flagged the projected lunar collision in April using publicly available tracking data. Jonathan McDowell, another independent tracker, was publishing the stage's trajectory through the spring. NASA's own CNEOS — the Center for Near Earth Object Studies — had confirmed 'a 100% chance of impacting the Moon.' By the time the stage hit on August 5, the collision was not a prediction. It was a scheduled event with a date, a time, and a location, published months in advance.

Against this record, the August 3 briefing is remarkable. SpaceX's representative described the impact as the product of 'a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces' — as if the trajectory were an act of nature rather than a disposal decision. The company said it had followed 'the appropriate rules and regulations' for upper-stage disposal. The rules were followed; the outcome was foretold. Both things were simultaneously true, which is exactly why the framing matters. 'Not deliberate' is true in the narrow sense that no one aimed the stage at the Moon. It is false in the only sense that matters: the trajectory was known, tracked, and published for four months, and no correction was made.

Then there is the concession buried in the same briefing cycle: for high-energy trajectories like this launch, deorbiting the stage 'is not possible.' Read plainly, this means the disposal method SpaceX described as compliant left the stage in an orbit that independent trackers — not adversaries, not leakers, just people watching public data — flagged as a lunar collision course in April. The company's own representative is describing a design limitation that made the outcome structurally predictable.

NASA's minimization deserves its own scrutiny. 'A meteoroid with the same energy hits the Moon about every six days' is a true statement that functions as a deflection. It conflates natural impacts with a man-made object whose trajectory was the subject of public tracking and prediction for months. The lunar surface absorbs natural impacts constantly. It does not absorb 4-ton rocket stages whose disposal paths were the subject of open-source analysis. The equivalence is rhetorical, not physical.

The physical evidence has now settled the matter. NASA's fresh imagery shows a ~60-foot crater at the predicted location. Korea's Danuri orbiter released before/after images of the darkened, cratered terrain. The impact occurred exactly where Bill Gray said it would, exactly when the trackers said it would. The crater is the receipt: the 'rare accident' was a predicted collision that happened on schedule.

The pattern here is the same one that shows up across institutional denial: when a failure was publicly foreseeable, the response is not to acknowledge the foresight but to redefine the event as an act of nature. Solar activity and gravity did not discover the Falcon 9 upper stage in April. Independent astronomers did — using data anyone could access. The 'rare accident' framing papers over a predictable disposal failure, and the crater proves it.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: The Falcon 9 upper stage impact was flagged in April by independent trackers using public data, confirmed at 100% probability by NASA's own CNEOS, and physically verified by a fresh 60-foot crater at the predicted site. SpaceX's 'rare accident' and 'solar activity and gravity' framing — plus NASA's 'every six days' deflection — paper over a predictable disposal failure. The concession says it all: for this class of trajectory, deorbiting 'is not possible.' They knew in April. The crater is the receipt.
